name: Marco Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lettings and property manager at the Eastfield branch of Brightwell Estates, a regional chain with about thirty branches. I look after around ninety rented homes for landlords, so my day is half lettings and half fixing things. Mornings are emails and repair jobs: a leaking tap on Corbett Street, a boiler that's died, a tenant who's locked out. Afternoons I'm out doing inspections or viewings. I like sorting a problem properly, and I don't like landlords who won't pay for a new boiler in January.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's a portal for repairs, and I use an AI chat tool now and then when I've got a stack of emails that all say the same thing. My colleague Dev uses it for everything, and I picked it up after I saw it didn't make a mess. I'm a solid manager, not the star of the branch, but my landlords don't leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that got oversold, which is what I'd guessed anyway. At work I'd say let's use it for the boring emails and move on. Online I'd say nothing, I'm not much of a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good news. My job's steady, the pay's good with the management fees, and my partner Leila and I can get on with buying a house. We've got about thirty-five thousand saved towards a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the job. Keep putting about six hundred a month into the house fund, so we can buy a two-bed next year. Maybe use the AI tool a bit more for repair updates, since tenants want to hear something fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. Just the usual pressure of house prices running ahead of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned house prices. Is that a real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it's the main one. Every six months the house my partner and I can afford gets a bit smaller or a bit further out. Leila teaches at a primary school, so she can't move too far from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to get that house sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We already skipped a holiday this year. I'd give up the car and get the bus, if it came to it. I wouldn't give up the gym, I'd go mad.

I'd suggest using it for **boring emails** and moving on.
think: I'd see it as **good news** for my steady job and pay.
Leila and I could get on with buying with **£35,000 saved**.
do: Put about **£600 a month** into the house fund.
Use the AI tool more for **repair updates** to tenants.
feel: He feels **calm**, with the usual pressure of **house prices**.
S0.quote: Every six months the house my partner and I can afford gets a bit smaller or a bit further out.
fieldNote: His main pressure is **house prices**, not AI.
He picks up tools **after a colleague** proves them.
He's proud that **his landlords don't leave**, which he sees as his real value.

steps.text: Put about £600 a month into the house deposit fund
Use the AI chat tool to send faster repair updates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's changing how we work and we'd better keep up. At work I'd tell the younger ones to learn the repair system properly. To friends I'd say it's good for tenants, mostly, because they'd get answers faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the lettings half of my job gets thinner. Booking viewings, chasing references, writing adverts, answering the same questions, that's what the card says AI takes. The repair and inspection half stays, so I'd be fine, but the branch might need fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the training on whatever Brightwell rolls out, and I'd use it every day. I'd push to take on more managed properties, maybe go from ninety to a hundred and thirty, because that's where the fees are. And I'd keep the house plan on track but maybe buy a bit cheaper, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for myself yet, but I'd watch the branch numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the branch would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kayleigh, our lettings negotiator, mostly books viewings and does the adverts, and that's exactly the work the system does. She's twenty-two, quick and funny. I'd try to get her doing inspections with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy cheaper if you think you're fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not certain, and a smaller mortgage means I don't panic if fees drop. Leila would agree, she's more careful than me. It's not a big change, maybe twenty thousand less on the price.

say: I'd say we'd better **keep up** with how work is changing.
I'd tell friends it's mostly **good for tenants**.
think: The **lettings half** of my job gets thinner.
Repairs and **inspections** stay, but the branch may need fewer of us.
do: Ask for **training** on Brightwell's new system and use it daily.
Grow his managed homes from **90 to 130**.
Buy a house **£20,000 cheaper** than planned, just in case.
feel: He feels **uneasy** and would watch the **branch numbers**.
S1.quote: Kayleigh, our lettings negotiator, mostly books viewings and does the adverts, and that's exactly the work the system does.
fieldNote: He splits his job into a **shrinking lettings half** and a safer repair half.

steps.text: Sign up for Brightwell's training on the new lettings system
Take on 40 more managed homes for the branch
Look at two-beds about £20,000 below the original budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government and the big firms to slow down and sort out support. At work I'd ask head office what happens to branch staff. Online, maybe I'd finally post something, probably about not leaving young people behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Brightwell closes half its branches within two years. An AI that answers tenants, books contractors, writes reports and negotiates rents does most of what I do at a desk. What's left is going round to look at a damp wall, and that's left only until the robots, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd do is put the house purchase on hold, which would be hard to say to Leila. I'd keep all thirty-five thousand in the bank as our cushion. Then I'd look into building maintenance or a surveying course, because someone still has to stand in a loft and say what's wrong, at least for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money and time, more than most, but the job I've built could shrink to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leila when you put the house on hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's rent one more year and see where we are. She'd be disappointed, because she's been looking at nurseries near the school. Not for a baby yet, just for the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is three years before robots enough time for the surveying plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tight. A proper surveying qualification takes longer than that. I'd go for something faster, like damp and timber inspection, and hope that buys me time.

I'd ask head office what happens to **branch staff**.
think: I think Brightwell **closes half** its branches in two years.

S2.quote: Someone still has to stand in a loft and say what's wrong, at least for a few years.
fieldNote: The **house delay** is the hardest part for him emotionally.
He sees the **robot gap** as too short for a full surveying course.

steps.text: Put the house purchase on hold and rent one more year
Keep the full £35,000 deposit fund as an emergency cushion
Take a short damp and timber inspection course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, if people start now. At work I'd push Brightwell to train staff for what's coming. To friends I'd say I'm thinking about my next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd see it as my warning to move. Five years is enough to get a proper qualification in building surveying, part-time. I'd still be anxious, because a lot of the surveying job is thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time building surveying course in the first year, evenings and some Saturdays. We'd still buy the house, but smaller, with a mortgage we could pay on Leila's salary alone if we had to. I'd use the AI at work every day, because knowing it well makes me useful whatever I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd feel like I was doing something. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said surveying is thinking work too. Why choose it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots come about three years after the AI. Half of building surveying is climbing into roofs and crawling under floors, so it buys me time past 2031. It's not perfect, it's just the best I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would buying on one salary mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-bed flat instead of a house with a garden, probably. Leila's okay with that, she grew up in a flat. We'd keep about fifteen thousand back as savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to plan, and I'd say firms like ours have no excuse. At work I'd suggest Brightwell plan which roles change. To friends I'd say get your house and your skills sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. I'd be 37 when it comes and 40 when the robots arrive. That's time to buy, settle and train for something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy the house next year as planned. I'd stay at Brightwell for a few years and aim for branch manager. Around year three or four, I'd start the surveying course, so I'm ready before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mild. It's a long way off and I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Leila change anything about kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe we'd have them a bit sooner, while both jobs are steady. It's not decided. Leila's school is one of the jobs I'm less worried about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What tells you when to start the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When Brightwell starts merging branches. If our Eastfield branch gets merged with the town centre branch, that's my sign. I'd want to be halfway through by then.

I'd tell friends to get their **house and skills** sorted.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would stop us buying a house and I'd have no time to train. What would help is cheaper part-time courses for hands-on trades like surveying, maybe with some pay while you study. And clear notice from firms like Brightwell.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about landlords. A lot of my landlords are retired people with one flat, and if agency fees drop, they'll go straight to an app. Some of them will be glad, and some will be lost.

headlineQuote: A lot of my landlords are retired people with one flat, and if agency fees drop, they'll go straight to an app.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old lettings manager** and property manager at a regional chain branch, looking after about ninety homes.
He and his partner Leila, a teacher, have **£35,000 saved** for a house.
He adopts AI tools **once colleagues prove them**, and sees his repair work as safer than lettings.
Faster AGI makes him **delay the house** and look at hands-on surveying work.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028**, which would stop the house purchase and leave no time to train.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **cheaper part-time courses** for hands-on trades, with some pay while studying.
